title: Secondary, composite and special indexes
subtitle: Pick indexes that match your real queries, read the plan to prove it, and count what every extra index costs on writes.

c.v: On 6 January 2026, GitLab.com slowed down for 2 hours and 36 minutes.
pipelines started late. Customers opened emergency tickets.
A background job queue grew to between 600,000 and 700,000 jobs. The PgBouncer
in front of the primary database was 100% full from 07:12 UTC. Database CPU stayed high.
The cause was one missing index. A migration after a deploy had removed
. That was a single-column index on
Queries that looked up signatures by

became slow or timed out. They held connections for longer, so the pool filled up, and everything else waited. By 08:51 the team had found the cause and recreated the index by hand. Performance came back.
One follow-up is the lesson of this page. GitLab updated its docs on the column order of
. The point: a query that uses only the trailing columns of a composite index is not covered by it.
The review does not say why the index looked safe to drop. But here is the lesson for you. An index can look like a copy of another one. It can still be the only one that serves a query.
A table stores its rows in one way. InnoDB keeps them sorted by
. Postgres keeps them in no particular order. A
is an extra sorted copy of a few columns, with a pointer back to each row. It lets the database find rows by something other than the main key, like orders by customer.
In PostgreSQL, every index is a secondary index. The rows live in a separate area called the
. A normal index scan reads the index, then fetches each row from the heap.

MySQL's InnoDB works differently. The primary key index (the clustered index) holds the rows themselves. Each secondary index entry stores the row's primary key. So a lookup finds the primary key first, then searches the clustered index for the row.
That is why InnoDB advises a short primary key: it is copied into every secondary index.
An index is a promise to answer one shape of query fast. You pay for that promise on every write. Choose indexes from your real queries, check the plan, and remove the ones nothing needs.

PostgreSQL states the exact rule. Equality conditions on the leading columns, plus a range on the first column without equality, narrow the part of the index it reads. Conditions on later columns are only checked along the way.
equality columns first, then the range column
. Winand shows the same with a date range and a subsidiary ID: with the equality column first, the scan reads far fewer index pages.
PostgreSQL 18 can sometimes "skip scan" past a leading column with no equality condition.
It usually does this only when that column has few distinct values. With many values, the planner usually prefers a full table scan.
The docs also say to use multicolumn indexes sparingly. Indexes with more than three columns rarely help.

q.v: You have an index on orders (customer_id, created_at). Which query can use it to read only a small, narrow part of the index?

why.v: Equality on the leading column plus a range on the next column gives one narrow range. A condition on created_at alone has no leading column to start from.

q.v: In MySQL's InnoDB, what does an entry in a secondary index contain besides the indexed columns?

options.v: The row's primary key, which is then used to find the row in the clustered index.
Nothing else. The index is only used to check uniqueness.

why.v: InnoDB stores the primary key columns in every secondary index record and uses them for a second search in the clustered index. A long primary key makes every secondary index bigger.

q.v: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows an Index Only Scan with Heap Fetches close to the number of rows returned. What is the most likely reason?

options.v: The index is the wrong type.
Many table pages are not marked all-visible in the visibility map, so Postgres still visits the heap for those rows.
The query has no WHERE clause.

why.v: An index-only scan only skips the heap for pages whose all-visible bit is set. VACUUM sets those bits.

q.v: You have a partial index ON orders (created_at) WHERE billed = false. Your app runs a prepared query with WHERE billed = $1 AND created_at > $2. Can Postgres use the partial index?

options.v: Not reliably. A plan made for any value of $1 cannot use it, because billed = $1 does not prove that billed = false.
Only if the table is small.

why.v: A partial index is used only when the query's WHERE condition clearly implies the index condition. Postgres docs say parameterized clauses do not work with a partial index. (Early runs of a prepared query may plan with the real value, but you cannot count on it.)

q.v: pg_stat_user_indexes shows idx_scan = 0 for users_email_key, the index behind a UNIQUE constraint on email. Should you drop it to save write cost?

options.v: Yes. Zero scans means nobody uses it.
No. It enforces the unique constraint on every insert and update, even if no query reads through it.

why.v: Postgres creates a unique index for each unique constraint, and that index is how the constraint is enforced. idx_scan counts only scans.
